opus-5.5.text:
I think the core idea is quite natural once you step back and think about how humans approach problems. If I ask you what two plus two is, you answer immediately. If I ask you to prove a hard theorem or debug a large codebase, you'll spend hours or days on it. The amount of thinking you do scales with how hard the problem is. Previous language models didn't really work that way: they spent roughly the same amount of compute per token whether they were answering a trivial question or something genuinely difficult. That's a pretty inefficient allocation.

What o1 and similar reasoning models do is let the model spend more tokens, and therefore more compute, working through a problem before committing to an answer. It can explore different approaches, notice its own mistakes, backtrack, and try again. On hard problems in math, coding, and science, that extra thinking translates into substantially better performance.

There are a few reasons I find this promising.

First, it opens up a new axis for scaling. For years the dominant story was scaling training compute: bigger models, more data. That's still important, but now we have a second lever, inference compute, and the two seem to be somewhat complementary. Some capabilities that would otherwise require a much larger training run can be bought, at least partly, by letting the model think longer at deployment time.

Second, it changes the economics. Not every query needs the same budget, so you can deploy a system that's cheap on easy tasks and only spends heavily where it actually matters. That makes it practical to apply these systems to really demanding problems without paying that cost everywhere.

Third, and maybe most important from my perspective, it moves us toward systems that can do long, extended chains of work, which is what you need for the kinds of tasks that matter economically: research, engineering, and multi-step projects. Much valuable human work isn't answering a question in one shot. It's sustained reasoning over a long horizon. If models can productively use more compute as tasks get harder, that's a sign we're getting closer to systems that can take on that kind of work.

There are open questions, of course. How far does this scale? Are there diminishing returns? How well does it transfer beyond domains like math and code, where you can easily verify answers? But as a direction, it seems both intuitive and empirically fruitful, and I expect it to be a big part of how capabilities progress over the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's interesting about O1 is that it introduces a second axis along which you can scale. Historically, the way we've gotten more capable models is by scaling training compute, so you train a bigger model on more data, and then at inference time you spend roughly a fixed amount of compute per token regardless of whether the question is trivial or really hard. That's kind of a strange way to allocate resources if you think about it. Humans don't do that. If you ask me what two plus two is, I answer instantly, and if you ask me to prove some theorem, I'll sit down and think for an hour.

What O1 does is it lets the model spend a variable amount of compute depending on how hard the problem is, and crucially, that compute is actually productive. You see these fairly clean scaling curves where performance on things like competition math or coding improves as you let the model think longer. So you now have two knobs: you can scale training, or you can scale inference, and there's some tradeoff between them. For a given level of performance, you could get there with a smaller model that thinks longer, or a bigger model that thinks less.

Why I find that promising is a few things. One is economic. Training compute is spent once, up front, and it's enormously expensive, and you're betting on the capability before you know what people will use it for. Inference compute you can spend on exactly the problems where it's valuable. If someone has a question that's worth a lot to get right, you can throw a thousand times more compute at it, and if it's a cheap question you don't. That's a much more efficient allocation.

The second thing is that it potentially relaxes some of the constraints people have been worried about on the training side, so things like running out of high-quality data or hitting limits on how large a single training run can get. If you can substitute inference compute for training compute to some degree, then those constraints bind less tightly.

And then the third thing, which I think is the most speculative but maybe the most important, is that the techniques you use to make inference-time compute productive, like search and self-verification and reinforcement learning on reasoning, those also generate data. So you can run the model for a long time on hard problems, get solutions that you can check, and then train on those. That creates a loop where inference compute feeds back into training, and that's the kind of thing that could compress timelines quite a bit if it works well. So I see it less as a single new model and more as the opening of a new frontier that we've barely started to exploit.

astra-6.text:
I think it opens up another way to improve these systems. Rather than relying entirely on making training runs bigger, you can give a model more time to work through a problem when it needs it. A straightforward question might require very little computation, while a difficult math or coding problem could benefit from much more.

That’s attractive because you don’t necessarily want to spend the same amount of computation on every question. You want to allocate it where the additional reasoning actually helps. If models can reliably turn that extra computation into better answers, then inference compute becomes another lever for improving capabilities, alongside training compute.

The important question is how far that scales: can you keep getting meaningful improvements by letting a system work longer? If so, that could be a very powerful direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it opens up another way of improving these systems. Previously, a lot of the progress came from spending more compute during training. But once you’d trained the model, the amount of computation it could use to answer a question was fairly limited, regardless of whether the question was easy or required a lot of reasoning.

With something like o1, you can spend more computation at inference time, allowing the model to work through a problem for longer. That’s appealing because different problems warrant very different amounts of effort. You don’t need a long deliberation to answer a simple factual question, but you might want substantially more computation for a difficult mathematical proof or a complicated programming task.

The promising thing is that, if that extra computation reliably translates into better answers, we have another dimension along which to scale capabilities. And we can allocate that computation to the problems where it’s most valuable. There are still questions about how well this scales and how the system decides when to stop, but it seems like a potentially important extension of the way we’ve been improving models.
